tasks.question: What are the main types of UK business electricity contract (fixed, variable, deemed, out-of-contract, flexible/pass-through, third-party-intermediary-brokered) and how do they differ in price certainty, risk and flexibility?

What practical preparations and wider considerations should a business address before signing (meter type and half-hourly settlement, contract capacity and usage data, timing of purchase, renewable or green tariff claims, Energy Bill Discount Scheme successor support, energy efficiency and reporting duties such as ESOS)?

Researcher notes: T1: Two sources were read: Ofgem (regulator, primary) and a broker blog (GLCG, commercial). Citizens Advice and Energy Ombudsman pages were not opened, because the search and page limits were used up. Ofgem's page gives no figures on the deemed/out-of-contract premium. A later task could add Citizens Advice or Energy Ombudsman detail on deemed rates, rollover and broker complaints.
T2: The page limit was reached. Not covered: objection rights (a supplier objecting to a switch), the 21-day switching timeline for non-domestic customers, the Energy Ombudsman's own guidance, the 2022 Microbusiness Strategic Review decision (removal of the fixed-term termination notice requirement), and the 12-month back-billing cap. These were seen only in search snippets and so are not cited. Licence condition numbers (for example SLC 7 and 7A) were not confirmed from a page I opened. Early termination charge amounts depend on the contract. The S3 and S1 pages show no publication dates.
T3: Gaps: no official source (Ofgem, NESO or a network operator) was read on the structure of network charges (TNUoS, DUoS, BSUoS), or on policy levies (RO, FiT, CfD, capacity market), or on recent changes to them. The only breakdown of these comes from the GLCG blog (S2). Ofgem bill-component pages in the search results were domestic-focused and not opened. Standing charges as a business bill element were covered only through the VAT treatment. Limits on page opens were used up.
T4: Not covered: how to check a supplier's financial resilience (Ofgem financial requirements, ratings, performance tables), and UIA accreditation and code-of-practice details (the UIA site was not opened). The Ofgem TPI page is from October 2022, so check it against the current rules from the April 2024 decision. Some Energy Ombudsman eligibility wording came from the broker page, and supplier-dispute eligibility was taken from Citizens Advice and Ofgem, not from the Ombudsman's own supplier page. Page-open and search limits were used.
T5: Not covered: government support schemes for businesses (Energy Bill Discount Scheme successor, British Industrial Competitiveness Scheme, etc.), any ASA or CMA guidance on green claims, how business customers should verify a green tariff, ESOS phase 4 details, and contract capacity and half-hourly meter specifics for customers. Page-open limits were used. A later task could target DESNZ and GOV.UK pages on business energy support and the ESOS phase 4 guidance.

metadata.rationale: All eight tasks have findings, and the core of the report is now backed by official sources. Ofgem and Citizens Advice cover contract types, renewal, switching and broker rules. The Energy Ombudsman covers broker disputes. HMRC covers CCL and VAT. NESO and Ofgem cover TNUoS, BSUoS and the Renewables Obligation. Elexon covers half-hourly settlement. GOV.UK covers ESOS phase 4 and BICS. The T6 to T8 follow-ups closed the main gaps: official network-charge sources, Ofgem switching and objection guidance, the 2022 termination-notice change, ESOS phase 4 dates, and a check on current support.
